title_en: Voster-Alps (USA) Trading Company v. Jiangyin Foreign Trade Company of Jiangsu Province — dispute over purchase and sales contract (appeal)
keywords_en: Civil; Contract Dispute; International Sale of Goods Contract Dispute; Second Instance; Supreme People's Court; Jiangsu Province; Legal Person; Foreign-Invested Enterprise; Foreign Economic Contract Law; Whether Discrepancies in Letters of Credit Affect Payment Obligation; Whether Goods Were Actually Accepted; Attribution of Liability for Customs Detention; Affirm the Original Judgment; International Sale of Goods; Letter of Credit Payment; Customs Detention of Goods; Import Agency; Dispute over Purchase and Sale Contract of Foreign Trade Company
full_text_en:
Voest-Alpine Trading USA Corporation v.
Jiangsu Jiangyin Foreign Trade Company
— Dispute over a sales contract

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Jiangsu Jiangyin Foreign Trade Company.
Legal Representative: Zheng Yuan, General Manager.
Agent ad litem: Xia Xipu, Attorney at Beijing Dingming Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Voest-Alpine Trading USA Corporation.
Legal Representative: Michael Hawker, Chairman of the Board.
Agents ad litem: Ma Qun and Sun Jinlong, Attorneys at Jiangsu Taihe Law Firm, Nanjing.

The appellant, Jiangsu Jiangyin Foreign Trade Company (hereinafter referred to as Jiangyin Foreign Trade), appealed to the Supreme People's Court against the civil judgment of the Jiangsu High People's Court in a dispute over payment for goods under a sales contract with the appellee, Voest-Alpine Trading USA Corporation (hereinafter referred to as USA Trading Company).

The facts found at first instance are as follows: On June 23, 1995, Jiangyin Foreign Trade entered into an agency import agreement with a third party, Gansu Guangxing Chemical Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Guangxing Company), stipulating that Jiangyin Foreign Trade would act as agent to import 1,000 metric tons of styrene; the port of destination was Zhangjiagang; on a CFR basis at USD 1,200 per metric ton; delivery was scheduled for July of the same year; upon arrival of the goods, Jiangyin Foreign Trade would promptly notify Guangxing Company, and Guangxing Company would, relying on the customs clearance documents handled by Jiangyin Foreign Trade, take delivery of the goods at the port area on its own; the agency fee was 0.8% of the total import value. On the same day, Jiangyin Foreign Trade entered into a contract with USA Trading Company, stipulating that Jiangyin Foreign Trade would purchase 1,000 metric tons of styrene from USA Trading Company (with a tolerance of 5% more or less); on a CFR basis at USD 1,200 per metric ton, with the port of destination being Zhangjiagang, China; shipment period was July 1995; payment was to be made by letter of credit, with an irrevocable letter of credit to be opened in favor of USA Trading Company through the Bank of China, Wuxi Branch (later changed to Jiangyin Branch) one month prior to shipment; after shipment, USA Trading Company was to immediately notify Jiangyin Foreign Trade by telegram of the contract number, commodity name, quantity, gross weight, vessel name, and sailing date. After the contract was concluded, upon application by Jiangyin Foreign Trade, the Bank of China, Jiangyin Branch, opened a letter of credit on July 6, 1995, for a total amount of USD 1,200,000. On July 11, 1995, USA Trading Company sent shipping information by fax to Jiangyin Foreign Trade, informing it of the vessel name, cargo, discharge port, discharge time, and other details. On the same day, Jiangyin Foreign Trade replied by fax: "Shipping information received, we confirm the above vessel, but hope to extend the discharge time to 24 hours; please load the vessel as soon as possible." The next day, July 12, Jiangyin Foreign Trade faxed Jiang Wenyuan, the person in charge of USA Trading Company's Shanghai office, stating: "Due to the recent sharp decline in international and domestic styrene prices, we will suffer significant losses. Please convey to your headquarters our careful consideration of the following proposals: 1) Given the current market changes, we are now unable to handle this business; we earnestly request that you postpone shipment, and the specific shipment date will be agreed upon separately. 2) Due to changes in customs policies, we are encountering difficulties in obtaining the duty-free import quota, causing us even greater losses. 3) We hope your company will consider the long-term cooperative relationship between both parties, agree to our request for a price reduction, and amend the letter of credit price." On July 21, 1995, Jiangyin Foreign Trade again faxed Jiang Wenyuan, stating: "Please contact Hong Kong and fax us copies of the certificate of quantity and quality within the next two days." On the following day, the vessel M.V. Duf Carmen, carrying the styrene, arrived at Zhangjiagang and began discharging cargo that same day, with personnel from both Jiangyin Foreign Trade and Guangxing Company present at the discharge site. On July 25, 1995, Guangxing Company, using the copies of the bill of lading, invoice, contract, and processing handbook provided by Jiangyin Foreign Trade, commissioned Zhangjiagang Ocean Shipping Agency to declare the goods at Zhangjiagang Customs. Customs at Zhangjiagang, in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Customs Law of the PRC, deemed that the consignee, Jiangyin Foreign Trade, had falsely declared general trade as processing trade with imported materials, which was suspected of smuggling, and therefore detained and controlled the cargo. On August 9, 1995, the Bank of China, Jiangyin Branch, received the documents from Texas Commerce Bank, USA. After examining the documents, the Bank of China, Jiangyin Branch, found discrepancies between the documents and the letter of credit and notified Jiangyin Foreign Trade and Texas Commerce Bank on August 1, 1995. On August 16, 1995, Texas Commerce Bank refuted the discrepancies pointed out by the Bank of China, Jiangyin Branch. On August 17, 1995, Jiangyin Foreign Trade faxed Jiang Wenyuan, stating: "Due to numerous discrepancies in the documents under the L/C, we are unable to take up the documents. Without taking up the documents, we will take no action regarding the cargo; the customs declaration has nothing to do with us." On the same day, Zhangjiagang Customs sent a letter, Zhang Guan Tiao (1995) No. 87, "Regarding the Agreement to Dispose of Styrene in Advance," to Jiangyin Foreign Trade, stating: "Regarding the 997.731 metric tons of South Korean styrene imported under your contract and letter of credit, carried by the M.V. Duf Carmen, which arrived at port on July 22, and is suspected of smuggling, this Customs, on July 31, 1995, notified Changshan Branch of Jiangsu Provincial Petroleum Company in writing to detain the cargo. Without Customs permission, no entity or individual may take delivery of this cargo. Given that styrene has a short shelf life and prolonged storage may cause deterioration, to avoid losses, this Customs agrees that your company should promptly sell and dispose of this cargo (price to be verified by Customs) and, in accordance with Article 22 of the 'Implementing Rules for Customs Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law of the PRC,' remit the proceeds to the account designated by Customs; otherwise, your company shall bear all liabilities arising therefrom." Jiangyin Foreign Trade did not dispose of the cargo as required by Customs, and on August 23, 1995, requested the Bank of China, Jiangyin Branch, to refuse payment of all amounts under the letter of credit. The next day, the Bank of China, Jiangyin Branch, notified Texas Commerce Bank and returned the entire set of documents. On October 16, 1995, USA Trading Company filed a lawsuit with the Jiangsu High People's Court, alleging that Jiangyin Foreign Trade had failed to fulfill its payment obligations, and requested that Jiangyin Foreign Trade pay the full amount of the goods and bear all litigation costs.

The Jiangsu High People's Court held that the contract between the parties was valid. Although Jiangyin Foreign Trade did not have the original bill of lading for the cargo, it took delivery of the cargo using a copy of the bill of lading and had stored the cargo in a designated oil depot. Jiangyin Foreign Trade raised no objection to receiving the cargo. When Jiangyin Foreign Trade, using copies of the bill of lading and other documents, attempted to declare the goods to Customs, the cargo was detained by Zhangjiagang Customs. At that time, the Bank of China, Jiangyin Branch, discovered discrepancies in the letter of credit and refused to pay. Jiangyin Foreign Trade's argument for refusing to accept the cargo on this ground was not supported. The letter of credit clause is a method of payment chosen by the parties; when there are defects in the letter of credit and the documents, the parties should negotiate a new method of payment, which does not affect the fulfillment of the obligation to deliver and accept the goods. Jiangyin Foreign Trade had actually accepted the goods and should bear the obligation to pay. The court, in accordance with Article 16 of the Foreign Economic Contract Law of the PRC, Article 15 of the Interim Provisions on the Foreign Trade Agency System of the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation, and relevant international conventions, ruled that Jiangyin Foreign Trade pay USA Trading Company USD 1,197,277.20 for the goods, and the case acceptance fee of RMB 59,697 was to be borne by Jiangyin Foreign Trade.

Jiangyin Foreign Trade appealed the above judgment, arguing that the trial court failed to ascertain important facts, leading to errors in findings. Jiangyin Foreign Trade's refusal to pay due to discrepancies in the letter of credit was justified. The taking of delivery and customs declaration were not actions of Jiangyin Foreign Trade; the contractual breach and violations by Guangxing Company were unrelated to Jiangyin Foreign Trade. Jiangyin Foreign Trade had not actually accepted the goods and should not be liable for payment. Furthermore, due to the improper detention by Customs and USA Trading Company's failure to take emergency measures regarding the goods, the subject matter had deteriorated, making it impossible for Jiangyin Foreign Trade to accept and perform the sales contract. Therefore, Jiangyin Foreign Trade requested that the court of second instance dismiss USA Trading Company's claims and terminate the sales contract between the parties.

USA Trading Company argued in response that Jiangyin Foreign Trade's attempt to shift responsibility by claiming that "the taking of delivery and customs declaration were not done by Jiangyin Foreign Trade, and Guangxing Company's contractual breach and violations were unrelated to Jiangyin Foreign Trade" was contrary to the facts and the law. According to the contract and legal provisions, the party obligated to fulfill the contract toward USA Trading Company could only be Jiangyin Foreign Trade. The relationship between Jiangyin Foreign Trade and Guangxing Company was entirely unrelated to USA Trading Company, and in fact, it was only after the dispute arose that USA Trading Company became aware of the agency relationship between Guangxing Company and Jiangyin Foreign Trade. After the conclusion of the sales contract and before the arrival of the goods, Jiangyin Foreign Trade had requested documents from USA Trading Company and was expressly informed of the time and place of the goods' arrival. After the goods arrived, the documents used for taking delivery and customs declaration—such as the bill of lading, invoice, and contract—were all provided by Jiangyin Foreign Trade. During the customs clearance process, Zhangjiagang Customs suspected smuggling and, in its letter of August 17 addressed to Jiangyin Foreign Trade, indicated that the goods had been detained by Customs and that Jiangyin Foreign Trade was responsible for their disposal. As for the discrepancies raised by the Bank of China, Jiangyin Branch, regarding the letter of credit, this occurred after the goods had been detained by Customs. The letter of credit was merely one method of payment; since Jiangyin Foreign Trade had already taken delivery and declared the goods to Customs, it was obligated to pay. The trial court's judgment correctly found the facts and applied the law, and USA Trading Company requested that the appeal be dismissed and that interest losses from August 9, 1995, be compensated.

The Supreme People's Court held that the international sales contract entered into by Jiangyin Foreign Trade and USA Trading Company on June 23, 1995, did not violate legal provisions, reflected the true and consistent intent of both parties, and was a valid contract. During the performance of this contract, USA Trading Company consistently provided the relevant documents and shipping information as requested by Jiangyin Foreign Trade via fax and was without fault. USA Trading Company had no legal or factual connection with Guangxing Company. Jiangyin Foreign Trade was aware of the arrival of the goods at the port and participated in the discharge. According to the contract between the parties, the Customs Law of the PRC, and the Interim Provisions on the Foreign Trade Agency System, Jiangyin Foreign Trade was the sole obligor under the international sales contract and was obligated to declare the goods to Customs and take delivery. Even under the agency agreement between Jiangyin Foreign Trade and Guangxing Company, the obligation to handle customs clearance rested with Jiangyin Foreign Trade. Although Guangxing Company commissioned Zhangjiagang Ocean Shipping Agency to declare the goods to Customs, the documents required for the declaration—such as bills of lading—were provided by Jiangyin Foreign Trade. Therefore, Guangxing Company's customs declaration should be deemed as having been authorized by Jiangyin Foreign Trade. Moreover, pursuant to the Customs Law, the consignee of imported goods is the legal applicant for customs clearance. It was precisely based on legal provisions that Zhangjiagang Customs, through its letter Zhang Guan Tiao (1995) No. 87, addressed Jiangyin Foreign Trade, requesting it to handle the goods in advance and bear all liabilities. If Jiangyin Foreign Trade disputed the detention by Customs, it could have initiated an administrative lawsuit; it could not, by claiming that Guangxing Company had commissioned the customs declaration, refuse to bear responsibility. Even if discrepancies existed in the letter of credit, that would only constitute grounds for refusing payment under the letter of credit, not grounds for the buyer to refuse the goods and ultimately refuse payment. In this case, the buyer, Jiangyin Foreign Trade, had already taken delivery of the goods but had not paid for them; its request to refuse payment was not supported. The trial court's findings of fact and application of law were both proper. USA Trading Company's claim for interest losses should be upheld. Jiangyin Foreign Trade's grounds for appeal lacked factual and legal basis and were not supported by this Court. In accordance with Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the Supreme People's Court rendered the following judgment on October 9, 1998:

1. Affirm the main text of the civil judgment of the Jiangsu High People's Court (1995) Su Jing Chu Zi No. 72;

2. Jiangyin Foreign Trade Company shall pay Voest-Alpine Trading USA Corporation interest on the principal of USD 1,197,277.20 (calculated from the date of refusal of payment under the letter of credit, August 23, 1995, until the date of actual payment, at the interest rate of the Bank of China for the same period).

The case acceptance fee for the first instance shall be borne as determined in the first-instance judgment. The case acceptance fee for the second instance, RMB 59,697, shall be borne by Jiangyin Foreign Trade Company.
